lead: At equilibrium two phases of the same mixture share the same temperature, the same pressure (when the interface between them is flat), and the same chemical potential for every component. Chemical potential μ<sub>i</sub> is the partial molar Gibbs energy in J/mol. It is the rate at which G changes, per mole of i, when a very small amount of component i is added. Fugacity f<sub>i</sub> in Pa is the working variable because μ contains an arbitrary reference term, and that term cancels only when the equality is written in fugacities. A phase is stable only if its Gibbs energy is a minimum, not merely flat. Distillation, extraction, crystallisation and refinery separations all use these tests.
prereq: You need the fundamental property relation dG = −S dT + V dP + Σ μ<sub>i</sub> dn<sub>i</sub> (from thermodynamic property relations) and chemical potential, fugacity and activity (from solution thermodynamics).

blocks.text: Start from the fundamental relation for a closed system of C components: dG = −S dT + V dP + Σ μ<sub>i</sub> dn<sub>i</sub>. Here G is Gibbs energy in J, S entropy in J/K, T absolute temperature in K, V volume in m³, P pressure in Pa, n<sub>i</sub> moles of component i, and μ<sub>i</sub> chemical potential in J/mol. μ<sub>i</sub> is also the partial molar Gibbs energy: the rate of change of G per mole of i added, at fixed T, P and other moles. At fixed T and P with no reaction, dG = Σ μ<sub>i</sub> dn<sub>i</sub>. Transfer dn<sub>i</sub> moles of i from phase β to phase α changes G by (μ<sub>i</sub><sup>α</sup> − μ<sub>i</sub><sup>β</sup>) dn<sub>i</sub>. If this is negative, transfer lowers G. Equilibrium needs it zero for every component, so μ<sub>i</sub><sup>α</sup> = μ<sub>i</sub><sup>β</sup> for every i and every pair of phases. Thermal equilibrium needs T<sup>α</sup> = T<sup>β</sup>. Mechanical equilibrium needs P<sup>α</sup> = P<sup>β</sup>. A curved interface can hold a small pressure jump because surface tension supports it.

blocks.where: μ<sub>i</sub> is chemical potential in J/mol; μ<sub>i</sub>° is the standard chemical potential in J/mol; R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; T is temperature in K; f<sub>i</sub> is fugacity in Pa; f<sub>i</sub>° is the standard fugacity in Pa. For the same component, the standard term cancels between phases, so μ<sub>i</sub><sup>α</sup> = μ<sub>i</sub><sup>β</sup> becomes f<sub>i</sub><sup>α</sup> = f<sub>i</sub><sup>β</sup>.

blocks.text: The fugacity form is the working criterion. It removes the arbitrary reference value inside μ. See 6.2 for counting the variables you may set, and 6.4 for using the equality in vapour-liquid equilibrium.

sections.h3: Stability: a minimum, not a saddle

blocks.text: At fixed T and P, a stable phase has the lowest G. For a binary mixture write g<sup>M</sup>/RT = x₁ ln x₁ + x₂ ln x₂ + A x₁x₂. Here g<sup>M</sup> is molar Gibbs energy of mixing in J/mol, R is the gas constant, T is in K, x₁ and x₂ = 1 − x₁ are mole fractions, and A is a dimensionless interaction parameter. The first derivative with respect to x₁ is ln(x₁/x₂) + A(1 − 2x₁). Setting it to zero gives a stationary composition. The second derivative is 1/x₁ + 1/x₂ − 2A. Stability requires (∂²g<sup>M</sup>/∂x₁²)<sub>T,P</sub> > 0. Because ∂²g<sup>M</sup>/∂x₁² = RT × d²(g<sup>M</sup>/RT)/dx₁² and RT is positive, the test is simply the sign of 1/x₁ + 1/x₂ − 2A. The spinodal is the locus where the second derivative is zero. The binodal is the locus of the two compositions joined by a common tangent to the g<sup>M</sup> curve; at those two points each μ<sub>i</sub> is the same in both phases, so they are the actual coexisting compositions. Between binodal and spinodal the mixture is metastable. Inside the spinodal it is unstable: any small composition wave lowers G, so the mixture splits without a nucleation barrier. Equality of chemical potentials is the criterion of equilibrium; this curvature test is the criterion of stability.

sections.h3: Using the criteria without mixing up variables

blocks.text: Use the criteria in order. First confirm T and P are equal; for a flat interface this is enough for thermal and mechanical equilibrium. Then write fiα = fiβ for each component; this is one equation per component. Finally check curvature. The equimolar point with A = 2.5 has negative curvature, so it cannot be a single phase even though its first derivative is zero. A = 1.5 gives positive curvature at x₁ = 0.5 and is locally stable. The same algebra appears in liquid-liquid extraction and polymer blends; see 6.7. For pure components the fugacity equality reduces to the vapour-pressure curve; see 6.3.

figure.caption: The worked examples on one curve: for A = 2.5 the Gibbs energy of mixing has two minima and a hump. The common tangent touches it at x₁ = 0.145 and 0.855, the two coexisting layers; the inflection points at 0.276 and 0.724 are the spinodal, and the equimolar point (curvature −1.0) is unstable.

examples.question: At 300 K and 1 bar, the molar Gibbs energy of mixing of a binary liquid is g<sup>M</sup>/RT = x₁ ln x₁ + x₂ ln x₂ + A x₁x₂ with A = 2.5. Test the equimolar mixture (x₁ = 0.5) for stability.
steps: First derivative: ln(x₁/x₂) + A(1 − 2x₁) = ln(1) + 2.5(1 − 1) = 0. The point is stationary.
The value is negative, so G curves downward at x₁ = 0.5. A small split into two compositions lowers G; the mixture is unstable.
examples.answer: The equimolar mixture is unstable because d²(g<sup>M</sup>/RT)/dx₁² = −1.0 < 0; it splits, and g<sup>M</sup>/RT at x₁ = 0.5 is −0.0681.
examples.check:
import math
A = 2.5
x = 0.5
x2 = 1 - x
d2 = 1/x + 1/x2 - 2*A
gmix = x*math.log(x) + x2*math.log(x2) + A*x*x2
print(round(d2, 4))
print(round(gmix, 4))

examples.question: For the same mixture (g<sup>M</sup>/RT = x₁ ln x₁ + x₂ ln x₂ + 2.5x₁x₂ at 300 K), find the two spinodal compositions and the compositions of the two liquid layers that coexist (the binodal).
steps: Spinodal: set the second derivative to zero, 1/x₁ + 1/x₂ − 2A = 0. With x₂ = 1 − x₁ this is 1/[x₁(1 − x₁)] = 5, so x₁(1 − x₁) = 0.2, or x₁² − x₁ + 0.2 = 0.

Binodal: the model is symmetric in x₁ and x₂, so the two layers are mirror images, x₁<sup>α</sup> = x and x₁<sup>β</sup> = 1 − x. The common tangent is then horizontal, and the condition is that the first derivative is zero at x: ln[x/(1 − x)] + 2.5(1 − 2x) = 0.
Solve by trial. x = 0.14: −1.8153 + 1.8000 = −0.0153. x = 0.15: −1.7346 + 1.7500 = +0.0154. Interpolating gives x = 0.145, where the sum is +0.0006, close enough to zero.

Check with activities, a₁ = x₁γ₁ and γ₁ = exp(2.5x₂²). Layer α (x₁ = 0.145): γ₁ = exp(2.5 × 0.855²) = exp(1.8276) = 6.22, a₁ = 0.902. Layer β (x₁ = 0.855): γ₁ = exp(2.5 × 0.145²) = exp(0.0526) = 1.054, a₁ = 0.901. The activities match, so μ₁ is equal in both layers.
examples.answer: The spinodal lies at x₁ = 0.276 and 0.724, and the coexisting layers are x₁ = 0.145 and 0.855. A mixture between 0.145 and 0.276 (or 0.724 and 0.855) is metastable; one between 0.276 and 0.724 is unstable and splits at once.

traps: Equating partial pressures p<sub>i</sub> instead of fugacities f<sub>i</sub>. At high pressure the fugacity coefficient φ<sub>i</sub> changes the answer: f<sub>i</sub> = φ<sub>i</sub> y<sub>i</sub> P in a gas.
Calling a mixture stable because the first derivative of G is zero. A stationary point can be a maximum or a saddle; the second derivative must be positive.
Calling the spinodal the phase boundary. The actual coexisting compositions come from the binodal, the common tangent where μ<sub>i</sub> is equal in both phases.
Using a pure-component standard state when the problem needs a Henry standard state for a dilute solute; the activity definition and the numerical fugacity change.

quiz.q: State the three equilibrium equalities for phases α and β.
quiz.a: Thermal: T<sup>α</sup> = T<sup>β</sup>. Mechanical (flat interface): P<sup>α</sup> = P<sup>β</sup>. Chemical: μ<sub>i</sub><sup>α</sup> = μ<sub>i</sub><sup>β</sup>, equivalently f<sub>i</sub><sup>α</sup> = f<sub>i</sub><sup>β</sup>, for every component i.

quiz.q: Why is fugacity used instead of chemical potential in phase-equilibrium calculations?
quiz.a: Chemical potential contains an arbitrary reference value. Fugacity is defined through μ<sub>i</sub> = μ<sub>i</sub>° + RT ln(f<sub>i</sub>/f<sub>i</sub>°). For the same component the reference cancels, so equality of μ becomes equality of f. Fugacity also has pressure units and connects directly to measurable P, x and y.

quiz.q: For a binary mixture, g<sup>M</sup>/RT = x₁ ln x₁ + x₂ ln x₂ + A x₁x₂ with A = 1.5. Compute the second derivative at x₁ = 0.5 and classify the mixture.
quiz.a: x₂ = 0.5. d²(g<sup>M</sup>/RT)/dx₁² = 1/x₁ + 1/x₂ − 2A = 2 + 2 − 3 = 1.0. The value is positive, so the equimolar mixture is locally stable.

quiz.q: At A = 2.5 and x₁ = 0.5 the first derivative is zero but the mixture is unstable. Explain what the second derivative shows.
quiz.a: The first derivative being zero only makes x₁ = 0.5 stationary. The second derivative is −1.0, so G curves downward there. Any small composition change lowers G, and the system lowers G further by splitting into two phases whose compositions lie on the common tangent.

quiz.q: Define spinodal and binodal in a binary mixture.
quiz.a: The spinodal is the locus where (∂²G/∂x₁²)<sub>T,P</sub> = 0. The binodal gives the compositions of two coexisting phases, found from the common tangent or equal chemical potentials.

quiz.q: A student finds μ<sub>i</sub><sup>α</sup> = μ<sub>i</sub><sup>β</sup> for every component but T<sup>α</sup> ≠ T<sup>β</sup>. Is the system at phase equilibrium?
quiz.a: No. Phase equilibrium needs thermal, mechanical and chemical equality together. If temperatures differ, heat can flow and G can fall; the chemical equality alone does not make the whole system equilibrium.

beyond: Not for the exam. The same curvature test predicts spinodal decomposition in polymer blends and metal alloys, and process simulators run a stability test before they report a bubble point or a tie line. Search next for 'tangent plane distance stability test'.
